newsitem.title: UK: Dlr lower in Europe, shrugs off Greenspan testimon.
newsitem.headline: Dlr lower in Europe, shrugs off Greenspan testimon.

text.p: The dollar was in consolidation mode in late European trade, taking a breather from its recent volatility and given little inspiration from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Senate testimony today.
The dollar edged back below 1.64 marks following Greenspan's prepared testimony which disappointed some by not commenting on current economic conditions.

"There was some disappointment but Greenspan would rather leave any dollar comments to the Treasury," said a Japanese bank dealer. "The market's consolidating now, we've probably already seen all the big moves we're going to see this week."

Greenspan did say in his testimony that a stronger dollar tends to restrain import prices but exchange rates "almost never" determine the outcome of Federal Open Market Committee decisions on interest rates.

The dollar also shrugged off a higher than expected U.S. weekly jobless claims figure which rose to 351,000 against 348,000 expected. A muted January APICS business outlook number also failed to stir the dollar.
By 1630 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6373/78 marks, off a session high of 1.6485 and below late Wednesday's European level of 1.6414/19 marks.
Against the yen, the dollar stood at 121.54/64 after holding territory above 122 yen and off late Wednesday's 121.89/94.

The dollar's slip late Wednesday and overnight was seen as shortlived by analysts and a necessary correction from this week's highs on the yen and mark ahead of key economic events next month, particularly the February 8 G7 meeting in Berlin.

"I don't think there will be a massive round of intervention from the meeting even if the yen hits 125, an historical G7 intervention area," said Claudio Demolli, forex analyst at Merrill Lynch in London. "The Japanese and German authorities are more concerned about the pace of the dollar rise."
The dollar was buffeted late Wednesday by comments from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer that the dollar's "normalisation" against the mark was near its end.

Overnight, dollar/yen was set back by comments from Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara who was reported to have said that Japan would intervene in the currency market at the appropriate time.

"I think we're getting to the stage where not just Japan but the U.S. and Germany are saying that this far is fine but any further would probably be problematic," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers.

Breedon said that even U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's remark overnight that the U.S. policy on the dollar has not changed -- a comment that had bolstered the dollar overnight -- could be interpreted as a watering down of his recent comments that a strong dollar was in the U.S. interest.
Elsewhere in Europe, the dollar was easier against the Swiss franc after a choppy session, ending the European session at 1.4219/29 francs from 1.4245/55 late Wednesday.
It was also lower against the French, shrugging off a five basis point cut in France's intervention rate to 3.10 percent. The dollar was at 5.5232/42 francs against 5.5420/30 Wednesday.
The mark also took the French rate cut in its stride and was marginally higher on the day from Wednesday levels.
The mark was a touch firmer against the lira but remained within the day's 980-84 lire trading range with activity much calmer after Tuesday and Wednesday's volatility.

Elsewhere on the crosses, the market was awaiting the outcome of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's summit with Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar in Bonn. The mark was slightly firmer on the peseta by late European trade.
